title: Why Checking Your Stocks Too Often Makes Them Feel Worse
audience: A curious adult with no background in this field

source.title: Myopic Loss Aversion and the Equity Premium Puzzle
source.authors: Shlomo Benartzi and Richard H. Thaler
source.venue: NBER Working Paper Series (Working Paper No. 4369)

intro.summary: This lesson draws on four sources to ask two linked questions: how much more do losses hurt than equal gains, and can that one bias explain why stocks have paid far more than bonds for a century? A large meta-analysis (Brown, Imai, Vieider and Camerer) pooled 607 estimates from 150 articles. It puts the average 'loss aversion coefficient' at about 1.96 (95% interval 1.82–2.11), a little below the famous 2.25, and possibly nearer 1.74 if missing low results are taken into account. Benartzi and Thaler's simulations show that a loss-averse investor who reviews a portfolio about once a year would find stocks and bonds about equally attractive. That matches the large historical stock premium without assuming extreme fear of risk. The main limits are these: the simulation shows the explanation is plausible, not that it is correct. Estimates of loss aversion vary widely between studies. Critics argue that loss aversion fades at small stakes, or that some effects reflect attention or inertia rather than losses weighing more. Topics covered only lightly here, and worth following up, include probability weighting, the endowment effect, loss attention, expectation-based reference points and the neural evidence.
background: Prospect theory, proposed by Kahneman and Tversky in 1979, says people judge outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point (such as what they have now), rather than by their total wealth.
The 'equity premium' is the extra return stocks have earned over safe assets: about 7% a year after inflation for US stocks since 1926, against under 1% for treasury bills.
A meta-analysis combines many studies' estimates of the same number, giving more weight to precise estimates, to find the best overall value and how much it varies.
Standard economics explains the premium by risk aversion, but the amount of risk aversion needed looks implausibly extreme.
intro.aha: The same loss-averse investor can find stocks unattractive or attractive depending only on how often they check them, and if people check about once a year, a loss aversion of about 2 is enough to explain why stocks have paid around 6% a year more than bonds.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Would you take a coin flip that wins $200 on heads and loses $100 on tails? On average it pays $50, yet many people say no. Their reason: losing $100 would feel worse than winning $200 would feel good. Psychologists call this loss aversion. These sources ask how strong it really is, and whether it can solve a famous puzzle in finance.
primer.quote: In cognitive science and behavioral economics, loss aversion is a cognitive bias in which the same situation is perceived as worse if it is framed as a loss, rather than a gain.

primer.heading: The puzzle
primer.body: Over most of the last century, stocks earned far more than bonds. To explain such a large gap, standard theory needs investors who are absurdly afraid of risk. Mehra and Prescott estimated a 'risk aversion' level above 30, where about 1 is considered realistic. So why does anyone hold bonds at all?
primer.quote: Since 1926, the annual real return on stocks has been about 7 percent while the real return on treasury bills has been less than 1 percent.

primer.heading: How big is loss aversion?
primer.body: Loss aversion is summarised by one number, λ (lambda): how many times more a loss hurts than an equal gain pleases. An early study of 25 graduate students reported 2.25, and many models still use it. A 2022 meta-analysis gathered every estimate it could find and combined them, giving less weight to imprecise ones. It found an average close to 2 (about 1.96). Estimates vary a lot from study to study, and a large 19-country replication found that the classic prospect theory choice patterns largely hold up.
primer.quote: We examine 607 empirical estimates of loss aversion from 150 articles in economics, psychology, neuroscience, and several other disciplines.

primer.heading: What Benartzi and Thaler did
primer.body: They added a second ingredient: how often investors check their results. Over short periods, stocks lose money often. Over long periods, they rarely do. Using real US returns from 1926 to 1990, they simulated a loss-averse investor and asked how often that investor would have to review the portfolio to find stocks and bonds equally attractive.
primer.quote: Second, investors are assumed to evaluate their portfolios frequently, even if they have long-term investment goals such as saving for retirement or managing a pension plan.

primer.heading: What they found
primer.body: The answer came out at roughly once a year, which is how often many people get tax forms and annual statements. With that review period, the best mix was about half stocks and half bonds, similar to what many real investors choose. If investors looked only every 20 years, a premium of about 1.4% would have been enough. The authors call the remaining 5.1% a year 'the price of excessive vigilance'.
primer.quote: Using simulations we find that the size of the equity premium is consistent with the previously estimated parameters of prospect theory if investors evaluate their portfolios annually.

primer.heading: Why it matters, and the doubts
primer.body: If this holds, part of the stock premium is a reward paid to people who can bear to look less often. But a simulation that fits the data is not proof. Loss aversion varies by setting and person. The meta-analysis finds hints that low estimates may go unpublished. Some researchers argue that losses mainly grab attention, or that people simply stick with what they have, rather than weighing losses more.
primer.quote: Multiple studies have questioned the existence of loss aversion.

concepts.title: Losses hurt more than gains feel good
concepts.idea: A value curve that is steeper for losses than for gains makes a loss of a given size feel about λ times worse than an equal gain feels good.

predict.question: Someone in this model has λ = 2. They lose $10 on Monday and win $10 back on Tuesday. Counting both feelings, where do they end up compared with before Monday?
options: Worse off: the pain of the loss outweighs the pleasure of the win
Exactly even: they got the money back
Better off: the win came last, so it counts more
It depends on whether $10 is a lot of money to them
why: Correct. The loss side is λ times steeper, so the $10 loss carries twice the feeling of the $10 win. The total feeling is negative even though the money is back.
That is how the money adds up. The curve scores feelings, though, and each lost dollar counts about twice, so equal amounts do not cancel.
Order plays no part here. Each change is scored from the starting point, and the loss side is steeper whichever comes first.
In this model pain is λ times the pleasure at every size, because the bend matches on both sides. Some real studies find less loss aversion for small stakes; that doubt comes later.

terms.means: The starting point that gains and losses are measured from. Here it is 'no change in money'.
Each extra unit of gain or loss adds less feeling than the one before, so the curve flattens.
Feeling a loss more strongly than a gain of the same size.
How many times more a loss counts than an equal gain. λ = 1 means no loss aversion. λ above 1 means losses loom larger.

model.title: How a win and a loss feel
model.note: Teaching model: it uses the 1992 prospect-theory value curve with the same bend (power 0.88) for gains and losses and a single multiplier on losses. It ignores how people weight probabilities and how people differ from one another. Amounts are illustrative units. λ = 2.25 is Tversky and Kahneman's 1992 median and about 1.96 is the meta-analysis mean, both as reported by Brown et al. All other numbers are illustrative.

steps.say: This curve shows how a change in money feels. To the right of the middle you are winning. To the left you are losing.
The middle is where you start: no change at all, and no feeling either way.
This slider sets how many times extra a loss stings. Watch the left side dive while the right side stays put.
These two sliders set the size of a win and of a loss. The dots show how each one feels.
These boxes read off the good feeling, the pain, and how many times bigger the pain is.

explore.prompt: Play with the sting and the two sizes. Can you make a small loss outweigh a big win, or find a win that makes up for a loss?

goals.text: Make a loss hurt more than a win twice its size feels good.
hints: First make the win at least double the loss. Then decide how much extra the loss must sting.
Doubling a win does not double its good feeling, because the curve flattens. So the sting needs to be a bit less than 2.
Watch the 'Pain ÷ good feeling' box. Raise the sting slowly from 1 until that box crosses 1. You will land somewhere between 1.5 and 2.

goals.text: With the extra sting at the 1992 estimate, find a win that feels at least as good as the loss feels bad.
hints: Set the sting to the 1992 value first. Then you need a much bigger win than loss.
Keep the loss small so the win has room to grow on the slider.
The win has to be well over twice the loss, somewhere between two and three times as big.

feedback.correct: Right. With λ = 2, the $10 loss carries twice the feeling of the $10 win. Ending up with the same money still leaves a net bad feeling.
feedback.incorrect: The money is back where it started, but the curve scores feelings, not dollars. The loss side is λ times steeper, so equal-sized losses and gains do not cancel. In this model that holds at every size.

steps.say: Start with no extra sting. A loss of 50 hurts exactly as much as a win of 50 feels good, so the ratio is 1. The middle point, where gains and losses are counted from, is called the reference point.

Double the win to 100. The good feeling rises from about 31 to about 58, which is less than double. Each extra unit adds less feeling. This is called diminishing sensitivity, and it bends both sides of the curve.
Back to a win of 50. Now give losses extra weight. The gain side does not move, but the loss side gets steeper, and the curve now has a sharp kink at the starting point.
The same 50 now brings 2.25 times as much pain as pleasure. Feeling losses more than equal gains is called loss aversion, and the multiplier is the loss aversion coefficient (λ).
The dashed line shows what losses would feel like with no extra sting. The gap between it and the solid curve is the extra pain that λ adds.
Shrink both amounts to 20. The ratio stays at 2.25. Because the bend is the same on both sides, a loss is λ times worse at every size.
Tversky and Kahneman's 1992 value of 2.25 came from 25 students. A later pooling of 607 estimates puts the average near 1.96. Losses still loom about twice as large.

understand.explanation: In prospect theory, people judge outcomes as gains or losses from a starting point, not as total wealth. The value curve rises for gains, falls for losses, and flattens as amounts grow on both sides. Loss aversion makes the loss side steeper by a multiplier, the loss aversion coefficient (λ), which puts a kink at the starting point. With the same bend on both sides, a loss of any size feels λ times as bad as an equal gain feels good. Tversky and Kahneman (1992) reported a median λ of 2.25 from 25 graduate students. Brown and colleagues pooled 607 estimates from 150 papers and found an average of about 1.96 (95% credible interval 1.82 to 2.11), with wide variation between studies. Some studies find little loss aversion for small stakes.
understand.quote: Empirical estimates of loss aversion are typically in the neighborhood of 2, meaning the disutility of giving something up is twice as great as the utility of acquiring it

connect.caption: This is equation (3) in Brown et al., following Tversky and Kahneman (1992). The coloured λ is the 'extra sting' slider: it multiplies only the loss side. The powers α and β make both sides flatten. The model fixes both at 0.88, the 1992 medians, so the pain-to-pleasure ratio for equal amounts is exactly λ. If α and β differed, the ratio would change with the size of the amount.

concepts.recap: On the value curve the loss side is λ times steeper than the gain side, so losses loom about twice as large as equal gains (λ around 2).

activities.prompt: Same win and loss of 50, two different stings. Compare the left side of the curve and the ratio box.
activities.takeaway: At λ = 1 the curve is the same on both sides, and a loss and an equal gain cancel out. At λ = 2.25 the loss side is more than twice as steep, so the same 50 hurts 2.25 times as much as it pleases.

concepts.title: Why people turn down a bet that pays on average
concepts.idea: A 50/50 bet is accepted only when the felt value of the gain outweighs λ times the felt value of the loss, so loss-averse people reject bets that have a positive average payoff.

predict.question: Some estimates in the meta-analysis fall below 1, which the paper calls loss tolerance. Take someone with λ = 0.8. On a coin flip they can win 50 or lose 60, so the average payoff is −5. Using the rule you just practised, what do they do?
options: Take it: for them the win feels better than the loss stings
Turn it down: the average payoff is negative
Feel exactly indifferent
Turn it down: losses always sting more than gains please
why: Correct. The rule compares the felt win with λ × the felt loss, not dollars with dollars. The win is worth about 31.3, and 0.8 × 36.7 ≈ 29.4 for the loss, so the bet feels slightly good even though it loses money on average.

This would hold for someone who judges only by the average payoff. The felt-value rule ignores the plain average. With λ below 1 the loss is shrunk, and that is enough to tip this bet into acceptance.
Indifference needs the felt win to equal λ × the felt loss exactly. Here they differ, at about 31.3 against 29.4, so the bet's dot sits a little above the line, not on it.
That is the typical case (λ > 1), but λ is a number that varies. When λ is below 1, losses sting less than equal gains please, and the same rule gives the opposite verdict.

terms.means: The average payoff of a bet if it were played many times; for a coin flip, half the win minus half the loss
A bet whose outcomes include both a gain and a loss; only bets like this reveal how big λ is

model.title: How a win and a loss feel
model.note: Teaching model: the same value curve as before (power 0.88 for gains and losses, one multiplier λ on losses), now applied to a 50/50 coin flip. Each outcome is weighted exactly ½, which ignores the probability weighting that real prospect theory adds. Amounts are illustrative units. Because the curve is a power curve, scaling both amounts by the same factor never changes whether a bet is accepted, so a win of 100 against a loss of 50 behaves like Samuelson's $200 against $100. λ = 2.25 (Tversky and Kahneman's 1992 median) and about 1.96 (the meta-analysis mean) are as reported by Brown et al. All other numbers are illustrative, not the papers' data.

outputs.label: How the whole bet feels (above 0 = take it)

steps.say: This is the same picture as before: the felt-value curve, with one dot for a win and one for a loss.
Now imagine a coin flip that pays the win or costs the loss. This new dot sits exactly halfway between the two, and it shows how the whole bet feels.
Watch its height. Above the 'no feeling' line, the bet feels worth taking. Below it, the person says no. The new number below gives that height.

explore.prompt: Use the three sliders to build coin-flip bets, and watch the whole-bet dot move against the line.

goals.text: Build a bet that makes money on average but that the person still turns down.
hints: The average payoff depends only on the two amounts. The felt value also depends on the sting.
First give the win a clear edge over the loss, so the average is positive. Then raise the sting.
With the win at its biggest and a loss a little over half of it, keep raising the sting until the whole-bet dot drops below the line.

goals.text: For a clearly loss-averse person (a sting of at least 1.5), set up a bet right at the edge: it is accepted, but a loss one notch bigger would get it rejected.
hints: You want the whole-bet dot just above the line, not far above it.
Pick a sting of 1.5 or more and make the win large. Then shrink the loss one step at a time until the dot first rises above the line.
Check the edge: if the next step up in loss would push the dot back under the line, you have found the largest loss this person accepts.

feedback.correct: Right. The decision comes from comparing the felt win with λ × the felt loss. When λ is below 1 the loss is discounted, so even a bet that loses money on average can feel worth taking.
feedback.incorrect: You probably judged the bet by its average payoff, or assumed losses always loom larger. The rule weighs the felt win against λ × the felt loss. At λ = 0.8 the loss of 60 feels like about 29.4, which is less than the win's 31.3, so the bet is accepted.

steps.say: Start with no extra sting and a fair coin flip: win 50 or lose 50. The whole-bet dot sits right on the line. The bet feels like nothing.
Make the win twice the loss: win 100, lose 50, like Samuelson's $200 vs $100 in $2 units. On average it pays +25, its expected value. With no sting, the dot rises above the line: take it.

Now give losses Tversky and Kahneman's median sting, λ = 2.25. The loss dot plunges and the whole-bet dot drops below the line. The expected value is still +25, yet the bet is rejected, just like Samuelson's colleague.
The rule: take the bet only if the felt win beats λ × the felt loss. Here 57.5 loses to 70.4. A bet with both a gain and a loss is called a mixed lottery, the kind of bet that reveals λ.
Shrink the loss to 40. The dot creeps up to just under the line, at −0.1. That is still a no, even though the win is now 2.5 times the loss.
One more step, to a loss of 35, and the dot finally crosses the line. With λ = 2.25, this person needs the win to be roughly two and a half times the loss before a coin flip feels worth it.

understand.explanation: A coin-flip bet feels like the average of its two felt values: half the good feeling of the win minus half of λ times the felt loss. A bet that makes money on average can still feel bad, because the loss is magnified by λ before it is weighed. So a person with λ near 2 turns down a 50/50 bet unless the win is about two to two and a half times the loss. Benartzi and Thaler open with Paul Samuelson's colleague, who refused to win $200 or lose $100 on a coin flip, and they use exactly this asymmetry to explain the refusal. The meta-analysis notes that only mixed bets, with both a gain and a loss, can reveal λ. This model is simplified: it weights each outcome by exactly ½ and uses one curve for everyone, while real people distort probabilities and differ a lot in λ.
understand.quote: Of more interest here is what the colleague offered as his rationale for turning down the bet: "I wont bet because I would feel the $100 loss more than the $200 gain.' This sentiment is the intuition behind the concept of loss aversion.

connect.caption: This is the meta-analysis's equation (2) for a mixed bet, w⁺(p)U(x) + w⁻(1−p)U(y), with U(y) = −λ(−y)^{β}. Here both decision weights are set to ½ (the model ignores probability weighting), and α = β = 0.88. The win x is the green slider, the loss −y is the orange slider, and λ is the sting slider. V is the whole-bet dot's height: take the bet when it is above 0.

concepts.recap: A loss-averse person takes a coin flip only if the felt win beats λ times the felt loss, so with λ near 2 they turn down bets that pay on average.

concepts.title: Combining 607 estimates: noisy ones get pulled in
concepts.idea: When many estimates are combined, each one is pulled toward the overall average, and the pull is stronger the less precise the estimate (larger standard error) and the more alike all the studies are.

terms.means: The typical size of a study's measurement error. A wide curve means a large standard error, so the study is less sure of its number.
How much the true λ really differs from study to study, beyond measurement error. Written τ; the paper's simplest model estimates τ ≈ 0.75.
The share of the gap between a study's reported λ and the overall average that gets closed: se² ÷ (τ² + se²).
Pulling each estimate toward the overall average when estimates are combined. Another word for pooling.

model.title: One study's λ, combined with what all the other studies say
model.note: Teaching model: one study is combined with a fixed overall average of 1.81, the value from the paper's simplest model (M1). The real analysis estimates the average and τ from all 607 estimates at once. The authors' preferred model also lets λ spread log-normally and groups estimates by paper. Curves are scaled so each peaks at height 1. The reported λ and uncertainty settings are illustrative and do not describe a specific study.

series.label: Where studies' true λ tend to lie

steps.say: The axis is λ, the loss-aversion number you met earlier. The blue curve is one study. Its peak sits at the λ it reported, here 5.
This line marks the average λ across all the studies, about 1.8.
This slider sets how unsure the study is. Watch its curve get wider.
This one sets how much studies genuinely differ from each other. It widens the dashed curve around the average.
The orange line is the study's combined estimate. This box shows how far it gets pulled toward the average.

explore.prompt: Play with one study that reports a strikingly high λ. Find out what makes the combination trust it less, and what makes it trust it more.

goals.text: Keep the study reporting λ = 5, but get its combined estimate below 3.
hints: Leave the reported λ at 5. What would make the combination trust this study's own number less?
Make this study more unsure and watch the orange line slide toward the average.
With the spread between studies left alone, the pull has to close well over half the gap. Look between 0.5 and 1.5 on the uncertainty slider.

goals.text: Leave the study's uncertainty where it starts, but get it pulled more than halfway to the average.
hints: You can't touch the study's own uncertainty. What else decides whether a λ of 5 looks believable?
Make the studies more alike by narrowing the dashed curve around the average.
The pull passes 50% once the spread between studies becomes smaller than the study's own uncertainty.

predict.question: Two meta-analyses each contain a study reporting λ = 3.5, with the same fairly large uncertainty. In meta-analysis A the studies disagree a lot. In meta-analysis B they nearly agree. In which one does that study's combined estimate end up closer to its field's average?
options: In B, where the studies nearly agree
In A, where the studies disagree a lot
The same in both, because only the study's own uncertainty matters
In neither, because a study's own result is never changed
why: Right. When studies are alike (small τ), the pooling factor se²/(τ² + se²) is large, so a λ of 3.5 looks out of line and is pulled most of the way in.
It can seem that disagreement should 'correct' outliers more. In fact a wide spread makes 3.5 a believable true value, so the pull is weaker in A.
The study's uncertainty is only half the formula. τ sits in the denominator too, and the two fields have different τ.
The reported number stays on record, but the combined estimate for that study does move unless its standard error is near zero.

feedback.correct: Yes. How hard a study is pulled depends on its uncertainty compared with the real spread between studies. When studies nearly agree, even a moderately noisy outlier is drawn strongly toward the shared average.
feedback.incorrect: The pull is se² ÷ (τ² + se²). With equal uncertainty, the field where studies agree (small τ) gives the larger pull, because an unusual value is less believable there.

steps.say: Start with a very sure study reporting λ = 5. Its narrow curve says '5, give or take a little'. The combined estimate sits almost on top of it: the pull is about 2%.
The width of the blue curve is the study's standard error, the typical size of its measurement error. Raise it to 0.5. The orange line slides about a third of the way toward the average.
Now a very noisy study, with a standard error of 1.5. It is pulled about 80% of the way in, because its data barely outweigh what all the other studies say.
The dashed curve is the between-study spread τ: how much true λ really differs from study to study. The paper's simplest model put τ near 0.75.
Make studies very different (τ = 2). Now a λ of 5 is believable on its own, so the same moderately unsure study barely moves: a pull of about 6%.
Make studies very alike (τ = 0.2). Now 5 looks out of line with everyone else, and the very same study is pulled about 86% of the way, to roughly 2.2.

The share of the gap that gets closed is the pooling factor: uncertainty² ÷ (spread² + uncertainty²). This pulling-in is called shrinkage. The orange curve is the narrowest: combining evidence also adds certainty.

understand.explanation: A meta-analysis cannot simply average 607 numbers, because some come from small or noisy studies. Brown and colleagues treated each reported λ as a noisy reading of that study's true λ, and treated the true λs as scattered around one overall average with a between-study spread τ. Each estimate is then pulled toward the average by the pooling factor se²/(τ² + se²), so noisy studies (large standard error) and fields where studies agree (small τ) are pulled hardest. In their simplest model this turned the raw mean of 1.97 into 1.81 (95% credible interval 1.74–1.88). Estimates with standard errors below about 0.4 barely moved, while very noisy ones, often the largest λs, were pulled strongly. Shrinkage is not a verdict that a big estimate is wrong, since a precise big estimate stays big. It also rests on assumptions (normal spread, independent estimates) that the authors then relaxed, which gave their preferred estimate of 1.955 (1.820–2.105).
understand.quote: estimates that fall far from the mean are shrunk towards more plausible values, with the amount of shrinkage proportional to the standard error.
understand.quote_where: Section 4.3 (Average Loss Aversion in the Literature)

check.task: Put the model in a state where a study reporting a large λ (4 or more) keeps nearly all of it: its combined estimate ends within 0.2 of what it reported.
check.hint: Pooling doesn't judge a number by how big it is. Ask what makes the combination trust a study's own result.
check.misconception: Large estimates are simply errors, so combining studies always drags them back to the average. In fact a precise large estimate is barely moved, because shrinkage depends on uncertainty and spread, not on size.

connect.caption: The paper's pooling equations (C.3) and (C.4). λ_{i} is the study's reported λ (blue slider) and λ̃_{i} is its combined estimate (orange). λ_{0} is the overall mean, fixed here at the paper's M1 value of 1.81. ω_{i} is the pooling factor, shown as 'Pull toward the average'. se_{i} is the study's standard error ('How unsure this study is') and τ is the between-study spread ('How much studies really differ').

concepts.recap: Combining studies pulls each estimate toward the average, more when it is noisy or when studies are alike. That turned a raw mean of 1.97 into a pooled 1.81.

concepts.title: How solid is loss aversion? The evidence and the doubts
concepts.idea: Loss aversion is widely supported (most estimates exceed 1; classic choice patterns replicate in 19 countries), but its size varies with stakes and methods, and rivals like loss attention and inertia explain some findings.

terms.means: Running an earlier study again, with new people, to see whether the same result comes back
When whether a study gets published depends on what it found, so the published record is skewed
The rival idea that losses make people pay more attention, without making losses weigh more than gains

concepts.recap: Loss aversion holds up on average (λ near 2; classic patterns replicate across countries), but its size varies with stakes and methods, and rival accounts explain some of its evidence.

understand.explanation: In concept 1 you met λ, the number that says how many times worse a loss feels than an equal gain feels good. A meta-analysis that pooled 607 estimates puts the average at 1.955. A large replication, which reran Kahneman and Tversky's 1979 choice questions with 4,098 new people in 19 countries, found the classic patterns again for 94% of items, though somewhat weaker. But the size of λ shifts with who is studied and how, and some studies find no loss aversion at all when the amounts at stake are small. Publication bias may push the average up a little, and two rival accounts compete with loss aversion: loss attention (losses grab attention without weighing more) and inertia (people simply stick with what they have). A fair summary is that loss aversion is well supported on average, but its exact size is uncertain, and some findings credited to it may have other causes.
understand.quote: Mkrva, Johnson, Gächter, and Herrmann (2019) cast doubt on these critiques, replicating loss aversion in five unique samples while also showing how the magnitude of loss aversion varies in theoretically predictable ways.

activities.prompt: Weigh the evidence one piece at a time. After each stage, ask yourself: does this make loss aversion look stronger, weaker, or just more complicated?

stages.label: 1. Pooling the literature
stages.text: Brown, Imai, Vieider and Camerer (s2) collected 607 estimates of λ from 150 articles reported from 1992 to 2017, in economics, psychology, neuroscience and other fields. The distribution of reported estimates has 93.9% of its mass above 1, the loss-averse side. Among the 419 estimates that came with standard errors, 398 (95%) are larger than 1. The authors' preferred model gives an average λ of 1.955, with a 95% credible interval of 1.820 to 2.105. That interval excludes 1 (no loss aversion). It also excludes the famous 2.25, which came from 25 graduate students in 1992.

stages.label: 2. Rerunning the classic study
stages.text: Ruggeri and colleagues (s3) directly tested Kahneman and Tversky's original 1979 methods with 4,098 participants in 19 countries and 13 languages. They adjusted only for current and local currencies, and every participant answered every item. The original results replicated for 94% of items and for 12 of 13 theoretical contrasts, 'with some attenuation', meaning the effects were somewhat weaker than in 1979. This tests prospect theory's choice patterns as a whole, not the size of λ alone.

stages.label: 3. Checking for a skewed record
stages.text: If studies that find loss aversion are published more easily than those that don't, the published average could be too high. The meta-analysis checked for this. A bias-corrected model gives 1.742 (95% credible interval 1.674 to 1.811). Unpublished working papers came out about 0.25 lower than published studies, roughly 1.73. The authors warn that their bias test may mislead, partly because λ must be larger than 0 by construction. Even so, the corrected values stay above 1.

stages.label: 4. The size depends on how you measure
stages.text: Estimates vary far more than chance alone would produce. Field experiments, general-population samples and means of individual-level estimates tend to give higher λ. Yet the coded study features explain only 15.5% of the variation between estimates. One survey that the meta-analysis mentions but did not include found a median λ of 0.99 in a representative sample of Americans, and 1.84 in a college sample using a highly similar protocol.

stages.label: 5. The critics
stages.text: Several studies found no loss aversion for small payoffs, a pattern called magnitude-dependent loss aversion. David Gal argued that status quo bias and the endowment effect are explained more simply by psychological inertia. Yechiam and Hochman proposed loss attention. In their account, losses raise arousal more than equal gains do: pupil diameter and heart rate rise more after losses. This happens even for small amounts where people show no loss aversion in their choices. In reply, Mrkva and colleagues replicated loss aversion in five samples and showed that its size varies in predictable ways.

activities.takeaway: Two strands of evidence point the same way: the pooled estimates and the cross-country replication both show loss aversion on average. Its size is less certain than the single number 2.25 suggested, and some of the findings it explains have rival explanations.

activities.title: Supports, challenges or refines?
activities.prompt: Put each finding where it fits best. 'Supports' means it backs the existence of loss aversion. 'Challenges' means it questions whether loss aversion is the right explanation. 'Refines' means it accepts loss aversion but adjusts its size or where it applies.

cards.text: 398 of the 419 meta-analysis estimates that came with standard errors (95%) are larger than 1.
cards.feedback: Supports. Across many studies and methods, nearly all estimates fall on the loss-averse side of 1.

cards.text: The original 1979 results replicated for 94% of items across 19 countries.
cards.feedback: Supports. A large, multinational replication of the founding study largely succeeded, though with some attenuation, meaning weaker effects than in 1979.

cards.text: Several studies found no loss aversion when the amounts at stake were small.
cards.feedback: Challenges. If loss aversion disappears for small stakes, it is not the universal rule it is often described as. Some researchers call it magnitude-dependent.

cards.text: Pupil size and heart rate rise more after losses than after equal gains, even when choices show no loss aversion.
cards.feedback: Challenges. This is key evidence for loss attention: losses can matter to the body and mind without being weighted more in choices. It offers a rival reading of some findings credited to loss aversion.

cards.text: Status quo bias and the endowment effect may be explained more simply by psychological inertia.
cards.feedback: Challenges. Gal argued that a simple tendency to stay put explains these patterns without any gain–loss asymmetry. That undercuts some of the classic evidence for loss aversion.

cards.text: Field experiments and general-population samples tend to give higher λ than lab studies with students.
cards.feedback: Refines. These findings do not question that loss aversion exists. They say its measured size depends on the setting and the people studied.

cards.text: Correcting for possible publication bias lowers the average from 1.955 to 1.742.
cards.feedback: Refines. You might call this a challenge, but the corrected value is still above 1. It lowers the size rather than removing the effect, and the authors caution that the correction itself is uncertain.

cards.text: The widely cited 2.25, from 25 graduate students, seems a bit too high next to the pooled average.
cards.feedback: Refines. The meta-analysis keeps loss aversion but updates the number that models and simulations often plug in.

hints: Ask of each card: does it doubt the effect exists, or only its size and where it shows up?
A finding that lowers λ but leaves it above 1 adjusts the effect rather than denying it.
Rival explanations for the same behaviour, such as attention or inertia, belong under 'challenges'.
activities.takeaway: Most of the large-scale evidence supports loss aversion. The doubts fall into two kinds: rival explanations for some of the same behaviour, and findings that the size of λ moves with stakes and methods.

activities.question: Having weighed all of this, which summary of loss aversion do you find most defensible?

options.text: It is settled: for everyone, a loss weighs exactly twice as much as an equal gain.
options.feedback: This reading has some support: the pooled average is close to 2, and the classic patterns replicate. But 'exactly' and 'for everyone' go beyond the evidence. Estimates vary widely between studies, one representative sample had a median of 0.99, and small stakes can show no loss aversion at all.

options.text: It is real on average, with λ around 2 in typical studies, but its size varies with stakes, people and methods, and some findings may have other causes.
options.feedback: This reading fits the most evidence: the meta-analysis, the 19-country replication, the variation between studies and the critiques. Its limit is that an average over very different studies does not tell you how loss-averse any one person or situation will be. It also leaves open how much attention or inertia explain.

options.text: It is mostly an illusion: attention and inertia explain the findings better.
options.feedback: The critics give real reasons for this view: no loss aversion at small stakes, stronger arousal after losses without loss-averse choices, and inertia explaining status quo effects. But these accounts explain some findings, not all. Large pooled and replication studies still find loss aversion, Mrkva and colleagues replicated it in five samples, and one can argue that loss aversion is the simpler account.

options.text: Nothing can be concluded, because the studies disagree too much.
options.feedback: The estimates do vary far more than chance would produce. But disagreement about size is not total uncertainty. The main credible interval (1.820 to 2.105) and the bias-corrected one (1.674 to 1.811) both exclude 1. That is real information about the direction of the effect.

concepts.title: One bet: no. Two bets together: yes
concepts.idea: Combining several independent bets and judging only the total makes losses rarer and smaller relative to gains, so a loss-averse person who rejects one bet can accept a bundle of them.

predict.question: Take the same person (losses count 2.5×) and a bundle of six flips, which they happily accept when judging the total. Now suppose they watch the result after every single flip and feel each win or loss as it happens. What does the model say about this way of experiencing the same six flips?
options: They still accept: it is the same bundle, and its total felt value is positive
They now reject it: each flip judged alone feels negative, so six such feelings add up to a clearly negative value
It comes out exactly neutral: watching closely cancels the gains against the losses
They like it even more: watching each flip gives them more chances to enjoy a win
why: It is tempting because the money at stake has not changed. But the felt value depends on what gets judged. If each flip is felt alone, the wins inside the bundle no longer cushion the losses.

Correct. Judged one at a time, each flip is worth 0.5 × 200 − 2.5 × 0.5 × 100 = −25, so six of them add up to about −150. Bundling only helps if the person judges the total and not the steps along the way.
Nothing in the rule makes gains and losses cancel out exactly. Each lone flip has a definite negative felt value under λ = 2.5, and adding six of them makes it more negative, not zero.
Watching more does show more wins, but it shows the losses one by one too, and each loss is felt 2.5 times as strongly. On balance, every flip seen alone is a net negative.

terms.means: How a person groups outcomes before judging them, for example flip by flip or as one total
The informal bookkeeping people use to sort, group and judge money outcomes

model.title: How good a bundle of coin-flip bets feels
model.note: Teaching model: every flip is an independent 50/50 bet to win $200 or lose $100, as in Samuelson's bet. The total is judged with the paper's simple rule: gains count once and losses count λ times (the paper's example uses 2.5). It leaves out the curvature and probability weighting of full prospect theory, and it allows at most six flips. Bars for win counts above the bundle size show zero. The $200/−$100 bet and λ = 2.5 come from Benartzi and Thaler's example. Other settings are illustrative, not the paper's data.

outputs.label: Chance the total is a loss
Felt value of the bundle (positive = yes)
Felt value of one flip alone

steps.say: Each flip wins $200 or loses $100, with even odds. Each bar is one way a bundle of flips can end, sorted by how many flips won.
A bar's height is how good or bad that ending feels, times how likely it is. Bars above the line feel good. Bars below the line are losing totals, which sting extra.
This slider sets how many flips are bundled together and judged only by their total. Watch the bars reshape.
This slider is the loss weight λ you met earlier: how many times worse a loss feels than an equal gain.
This box adds every bar together. Above zero, the person says yes to the bundle. Below zero, they say no.

explore.prompt: Keep the paper's loss weight and play with the bundle size. Watch how the losing bars shrink and when the felt value flips sign.

goals.text: Keeping the loss weight at the paper's 2.5, find the smallest bundle of flips that this person would accept.
hints: Leave λ alone. Only the number of flips needs to change.
Add flips one at a time and watch the felt value box after each step.
You don't need a big bundle. Try the very first sizes above a single flip.

feedback.correct: Right. What matters is what gets judged. Felt one flip at a time, every flip is a −25 experience under λ = 2.5, so six of them feel clearly bad. The same six flips judged as one total feel clearly good.
feedback.incorrect: You probably assumed that the money decides. In this model, the grouping decides. A bundle only cushions losses with wins if the person looks at the total. Watched flip by flip, each loss is felt on its own at 2.5 times its size, and each lone flip feels like −25.

steps.say: Start with one flip and λ = 2.5. Half the time you gain $200 (feels like +200). Half the time you lose $100 (feels like −250). Averaged: 100 − 125 = −25. The person says no.
Yet this flip pays $50 on average. As you saw before, a loss-averse person turns down a bet that pays on average.
Now bundle three flips and judge only the total. Ending with a loss now requires all three flips to lose, which happens only 1 time in 8. One win plus two losses breaks exactly even.
The losing bar is shorter, and the winning bars have grown. The pain from losses is about 94, against about 188 of good feeling. The felt value is now positive. The flips themselves did not change.
This is an aggregation rule at work: the way outcomes are grouped before judging them. It is part of mental accounting. Inside a bundle, wins quietly cancel losses before anything is judged.
Bundle six flips. A losing total now happens only about 11% of the time, and the felt value climbs well above zero.
Now make losses hurt more, at λ = 4. One flip alone now feels like −100, but the six-flip bundle still feels clearly good. The same bet gets opposite answers depending on how it is grouped.

understand.explanation: Benartzi and Thaler start from Samuelson's colleague, who refused one 50/50 bet to win $200 or lose $100 but would take a hundred of them. With losses counted 2.5 times, one flip feels like −25. Two flips judged as a single total lose money only 1 time in 4, and the felt value becomes +25. Bundling changes nothing about any flip. It changes what gets judged: inside the total, wins offset losses, so losing totals become rarer and smaller relative to the gains. The paper shows this with simple arithmetic on its toy utility function, so it is a worked example, not a measured result. Under standard expected-utility theory this yes-to-many, no-to-one pattern counts as inconsistent, and the trend is not perfectly smooth: four flips can end in a loss more often than three.
understand.quote: The distribution of outcomes created by the portfolio of two bets {$400, .25; 100, .50; -$200, .25) yields positive expected utility with the hypothesized utility function, though of course simple repetitions of the single bet are unattractive if evaluated one at a time.

check.task: Someone claims: 'If you refuse one bet, you must refuse any bundle of copies of it.' Prove them wrong for a person whose losses weigh at least 6 times as much as gains. Put the model in a state where this person turns down one flip on its own but accepts the bundle.
check.hint: Push the loss weight to the top of its range. Then try bundle sizes from small to large and watch the felt value box. Small bundles are not enough at this weight.
check.misconception: Believing that the same bet must always get the same answer. In fact, the answer depends on whether each bet is judged alone or only as part of a total, because inside a bundle the wins offset the losses before they are felt.

connect.caption: U is the paper's simple utility function: gains count once, losses count λ times (the paper writes 2.5x). The bundle sum is the model's rule, not an equation printed in the paper. k is the number of winning flips, 300k − 100n is the total in dollars for n flips, and p_{k} = binom(n, k)/2^{n} is its chance. Each bar is one term of the sum, and the felt value box is V.

concepts.recap: Judge many bets as one total and wins cushion losses, so a loss-averse person who refuses one bet can welcome a bundle of them, but only if they don't feel each flip separately.

concepts.title: How often you check decides whether stocks feel worth it
concepts.idea: The longer the evaluation period, the less often a risky asset shows a loss, so for a loss-averse investor its felt value rises above a safe asset's once the period is long enough.

predict.question: A second investor feels losses even more sharply than the first: λ = 3 instead of 2.25. The stock and the safe asset are the same. What happens to the shortest checking interval at which stocks feel worth holding?
options: It gets longer: this investor must check less often before stocks win
It gets shorter: this investor can check more often
It stays the same, because λ does not change the returns
Stocks can never beat the safe asset for this investor
why: Right. Each loss that a check shows now weighs 3 times as much. The stock needs a lower chance of showing a loss, and only a longer interval between checks delivers that. In this model the crossover moves from about 10 months to roughly 16–17 months.
This is tempting if you think a stronger reaction makes someone a more careful investor. A bigger λ makes every visible loss cost more, so stocks need more time between checks to win, not less.
The returns are indeed unchanged, but felt value depends on how losses are weighed as well as on the returns. Raising λ pulls the stock curve down at every interval, so the crossing point moves.

A bigger λ lowers the stock curve but does not keep it down forever. Losses keep getting rarer as the interval grows, so even a very loss-averse investor ends up preferring stocks if they check rarely enough.

terms.means: How much time passes between the moments when an investor looks at their returns and judges them as gains or losses
Benartzi and Thaler's name for loss aversion combined with frequent checking, which makes risky assets feel worse than they are over the long run

model.title: How good a stock and a safe asset feel, depending on how often you check
model.note: Teaching model, simplified in four ways. (1) Returns over each checking interval are normal, with an 8% mean and a 20% spread per year; this is the illustrative stock in the paper's introduction. (2) The safe asset pays a sure 1% a year. (3) Felt value uses a two-slope curve, where gains count once and losses count λ times, with true probabilities. (4) Values are shown per year of holding so the safe line stays flat; at very short intervals the stock curve falls off the bottom of the chart. The paper instead resampled real 1926–1990 US returns and used the full prospect-theory curves. It found a crossover of 9–12 months, or 8 months with the simple two-slope curve. The numbers here are illustrative, not the paper's data.

outputs.label: Safe asset: felt value per year
Chance a check shows a loss

x.label: How often you check (months between looks)

steps.say: This curve shows how good a stock feels per year to someone who dislikes losses. It depends on how often they look at it.
The dashed line is a safe asset paying a sure 1% a year. It never shows a loss, so it always feels like 1%.
This slider sets how many months pass between looks. The marker moves with it.
This slider sets λ: how many times worse a loss feels than an equal gain feels good.
These boxes read out both felt values at your interval, plus the chance that a single look shows a loss.

explore.prompt: Keep λ at 2.25 and play with how often you check. Find the point where holding stocks starts to feel better than the safe asset.

goals.text: With λ at 2.25, find the shortest checking interval (in whole months) at which stocks feel better than the safe asset.
hints: Stocks win when losses show up rarely enough. Which slider changes how often a look shows a loss?
Leave λ alone and lengthen the interval one month at a time, watching the 'Stocks minus safe' box.
The walkthrough had stocks losing at 6 months and winning at 12. The switch happens in between, so find the first month where the gap turns positive.

feedback.correct: Yes. A bigger λ makes each visible loss cost more, so the stock needs an even lower chance of showing a loss. Only a longer interval between checks delivers that, so the crossover moves later.
feedback.incorrect: λ does not change the returns, but it changes how much each loss you see hurts. With λ = 3 the stock curve sits lower at every interval, so it meets the safe line further to the right. Stocks still win eventually, because losses keep getting rarer as the interval grows.

steps.say: Start with λ = 1, so losses and gains count equally. The stock feels like its plain 8% average however often you look, far above the safe 1%.
Now set λ = 2.25, the median Tversky and Kahneman reported. If you look every month, about 45% of looks show a loss. Each one stings 2.25 times as much, so stocks feel far worse than the safe asset.
The time between looks is the evaluation period. Stretch it to 6 months and the chance of seeing a loss falls to about 39%. Stocks still feel worse than a sure 1%.
Why does waiting help? The average gain grows in step with time, but the spread grows only with its square root. Over longer periods the gain outruns the swings.
At a 12-month evaluation period only about a third of looks show a loss. The stock curve has climbed above the safe line, so a yearly checker would rather hold stocks.
Look every two years and fewer than 30% of looks show a loss. Stocks now feel worth almost 5% a year, against the safe asset's 1%.

Nothing changed about the stock or the investor, only the habit of looking. Benartzi and Thaler call loss aversion plus frequent looking myopic loss aversion. Here the curves cross somewhere between 6 and 12 months.

understand.explanation: If you check a risky investment often, many checks show a loss. With λ near 2, each loss stings more than twice as much as an equal gain pleases, so the stock feels worse than a safe 1%. Over a longer evaluation period the average gain builds faster than the swings, so fewer checks show a loss and the stock's felt value climbs until it crosses the safe line. Benartzi and Thaler tested this by drawing from real 1926–1990 US returns and scoring them with Tversky and Kahneman's prospect-theory parameters. They found the crossover at about one year, or about 8 months with a simple two-slope curve. They present this as a plausibility check, not a proof: it shows the idea fits the numbers. They also note that real investors may look at several intervals at once.
understand.quote: As the figures show, the horizon at which the prospective utility for stocks is equal to the value for bonds or treasury bills is always between 9 and 12 months, or roughly one year.

connect.caption: This is the model's rule, not the paper's full prospect-theory formula. It uses the two-slope value curve from the paper's sensitivity check: gains count once, losses count λ times, and probabilities are the true ones. V is the stock's felt value over one evaluation period T (the checking-interval slider, in years here). The model divides V by T to show it per year. The minus-one term is the extra sting of the loss part, and it shrinks as T grows. λ is the loss-aversion slider.

concepts.recap: Checking less often hides most losses, so a loss-averse investor who looks yearly rather than monthly can find stocks worth holding.

concepts.title: The equity premium as the price of looking too often
concepts.idea: The stock premium needed to make a loss-averse investor indifferent between stocks and bonds falls steeply as the evaluation period lengthens, and a one-year period with λ near 2 matches the roughly 6.5% premium actually seen.

predict.question: A large meta-analysis puts the average loss aversion λ near 1.96, a bit lower than the 2.25 used in this model. For an investor who checks once a year, how big an extra return would stocks need so that they feel exactly as good as the sure 1%?
options: A smaller extra return than about 6%
A larger extra return than about 6%
The same: λ doesn't affect the balance point
No extra return would ever be enough
why: Right. A lower λ means each loss stings less, so stocks need less extra return to make up for the losing years. In this toy the balance moves from about 6.1% to about 5%.
That would hold if λ went up. A smaller λ shrinks the penalty on losing years, so stocks feel better and need less extra return to break even.
λ is exactly what sets how hard the losing years hit. Change it and the stocks curve moves, so the balance point moves too.
Even at λ = 1.95, a yearly checker sees a loss only some of the time. A big enough extra return always lifts stocks above the sure 1%, as the slider shows.

terms.means: The extra average yearly return that stocks pay over safe assets such as bonds
The paper's name for the 5.1% a year that yearly checking costs a 20-year investor: the 6.5% premium a yearly checker needs minus the 1.4% a 20-year checker would need
Liking two options exactly equally, so neither choice feels better

model.title: How much extra return stocks need, depending on how often you check
model.note: Teaching model: the same simplified picture as before, plus one new slider. (1) Stock returns over each checking interval are normal with a 20% yearly spread. Their average is the safe 1% plus the extra-return slider; at 7%, this is the 8% stock the paper uses as an example in its introduction. (2) The safe asset pays a sure 1% a year. (3) Felt value uses the two-slope curve (gains count once, losses count λ times) with true probabilities, shown per year of holding. (4) The checking slider stops at 36 months, so the paper's 5-, 10- and 20-year results are quoted, not shown. The paper instead drew samples from real 1926–1990 US monthly returns, compared stocks with 5-year bonds for this analysis, and used full prospect theory (λ = 2.25, curvature 0.88, decision weights). In this toy, a yearly checker with λ = 2.25 balances at an extra return of about 6.1%. The paper's simulation found the actual 6.5% premium consistent with a one-year period. All curve values here are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: Stocks' extra yearly return over the safe asset

steps.say: Same picture as before. The solid curve is how good stocks feel at each checking interval, the dashed line is the sure 1%, and the vertical line marks how often you look.
One new slider: how much more stocks earn on average each year than the safe asset. Raise it and the whole stocks curve lifts.
Lower it and the curve sinks. Wherever the curve crosses the dashed line, stocks and the sure thing feel the same.

explore.prompt: You're the market. Find how much extra return stocks must pay before a loss-averse person (λ = 2.25) is happy to hold them. Do it first for someone who checks once a year, then for someone who checks only every three years.

goals.text: Keep λ at 2.25. For someone who checks once a year, find the extra return that makes stocks and the safe asset feel equal (gap within ±0.15%).
hints: First set the checking slider to match someone who looks once a year.
Then move the extra-return slider and watch the 'Stocks minus safe' box head toward zero.
The balance sits between 5% and 7%. Nudge in small steps until the stocks point lands on the dashed line.

goals.text: Keep λ at 2.25. Now find the extra return that makes stocks and the safe asset feel equal for someone who checks only every 3 years (gap within ±0.15%).
hints: Three years is the longest interval this slider allows.
Checking that rarely makes the stocks point jump up, so you'll need to lower the extra return, not raise it.
The answer is well below 5% but more than half of your yearly answer. Use small steps and watch the gap.

feedback.correct: Yes. λ sets how much the losing years hurt. With λ near 1.96 they hurt less, so in this toy a yearly checker needs a smaller extra return: about 5% rather than about 6.1%. The exact match to the real premium depends on which λ you trust.
feedback.incorrect: You may have expected λ to make no difference, or to push the answer up. The balance comes from weighing gains against λ times the losses. A smaller λ shrinks the loss side, so stocks need less extra return before they feel as good as the sure 1%.

steps.say: Take someone with λ = 2.25 who checks once a year. With stocks earning 7% more than the safe asset each year, the stocks point sits above the dashed line, so stocks feel better.

That extra average yearly return of stocks over a safe asset is called the equity premium. Lower it until the point sits on the dashed line. At about 6.1%, this person is indifferent: stocks and the sure thing feel equal.
Keep that same 6.1% premium, but now check only every 3 years. The point leaps well above the line. Fewer looks mean fewer losing reports, so the same premium is now more than enough.
So how much does a 3-year checker actually need? Lower the premium until the point is back on the line: only about 3.4%. The longer the evaluation period, the smaller the premium needed.
The paper ran this with real 1926–1990 returns. The premium consistent with each period fell from 6.5% at one year to 4.65% at two years, 3% at five, 2% at ten and 1.4% at twenty.

For a 20-year investor, checking yearly costs about 5.1% a year (6.5% minus 1.4%): the paper's price of excessive vigilance. Back at a yearly check here, 3.4% makes stocks feel worse than the sure 1%.
Put in the real premium, about 6.5%. In this toy, a yearly checker with λ ≈ 2.35 is indifferent; the paper's full model matched it with 2.25. Yearly looks plus λ near 2 can explain a ~6% premium.

understand.explanation: Turn the earlier question around. Instead of asking whether stocks feel worth it, ask how big the equity premium must be to make a loss-averse person indifferent. The answer shrinks fast as the evaluation period grows, because rare looks rarely show a loss. Benartzi and Thaler simulated this with real 1926–1990 US returns on stocks and 5-year bonds, using prospect theory's previously estimated parameters rather than ones selected to fit the data best. They found the observed 6.5% premium consistent with a one-year evaluation period, and found it would fall to 1.4% for a 20-year one. That 5.1% gap is what they call the 'price of excessive vigilance'. The match is suggestive, not proof: the authors note there is no way of demonstrating that one particular explanation is correct. The numbers also depend on the details. Their simple two-slope version with true probabilities needed λ = 2.77 for a 12-month period, while a later meta-analysis puts average λ near 1.96 (about 1.74 after correcting for possible publication bias).
understand.quote: With the parameters we have been using, the actual equity premium in our data (6.5 percent per year) is consistent with an evaluation period of one year. If the evaluation period were 2 years, the equity premium would fall to 4.65 percent. For 5, 10, and 20 year evaluation periods, the corresponding figures are 3.0 percent, 2.0 percent, and 1.4 percent.
understand.quote_where: Section 5, Myopia and the Magnitude of the Equity Premium

equation.text: ) = V_{safe}(T),   where V = Σ p_{i}·v(x_{i}) and v(x) = x if x ≥ 0,

connect.caption: The paper seeks the premium at which the prospect value of stocks over an evaluation period T equals that of bonds. V(G) = Σ π_{i} v(x_{i}); its simple check uses v(x) = x for gains and 2.25x for losses with true probabilities. T is the checking slider, the premium is the new slider, and λ is the loss-aversion slider. The model plots V per year as the 'Stocks' curve. The full version adds curvature (x^{0.88}) and decision weights π_{i}.

concepts.recap: The extra return stocks must pay falls steeply as you check less often; a yearly check with λ near 2 fits the real ~6.5% equity premium, the price of looking too often.
